Quirk Genetics and Inheritance.text: Quirks run in families. A child's Quirk usually takes after one parent's, mixes features of both, or turns out as something new that grows out of the family's traits. The child of a parent who hardens their skin and a parent who breathes underwater may inherit either power, a blend of the two or something neither parent has. Mutation happens too: parents with ordinary-looking bodies can have a heteromorph child, or a child with a power that has no clear family source, and doctors treat this as normal variation. Families with famous Quirks draw close attention from the press and from agencies watching for the next generation of talent. Choosing a partner for the power a child might inherit is called a Quirk marriage. It was common in the early generations and some old families still arrange them quietly, but the public now treats the practice as a scandal: marrying for a Quirk means treating a spouse and children as a breeding project, and any public figure suspected of it pays in reputation. Most families simply hope a child's Quirk turns out safe, useful and easy to live with. No test can promise a particular result before a child is born, and two siblings raised in the same house can have entirely different powers.
